delta_method: F1 wording; F2 syntax/idiom; F3 consequential interpretive or textual choice. Labels are editorial assessments, not generated from similarity. All current wording and notes require editorial review.

verses.rationale: Make the epistolary greeting a complete English sentence; retain twelve tribes and servant rather than replacing the addressees with a modern church category.
verses.before: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes in the dispersion: greetings.
verses.after: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, sends greetings to the twelve tribes scattered abroad.
verses.tsw_comparator: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes in the dispersion: greetings.

verses.rationale: Reorder the address and circumstance into a complete exhortation; preserve the surprising command about joy without explaining away suffering.
verses.before: Consider it pure joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you encounter various trials,
verses.after: My brothers and sisters, when you meet trials of every kind, count it all as joy.
verses.tsw_comparator: Count it all joy, my brothers and sisters, when you fall into trials of various kinds,

verses.rationale: Use an English verbal construction for the testing of faith; retain the causal movement into endurance.
verses.before: because you know that the testing of your faith produces endurance.
verses.after: You know that having your faith tested develops endurance.
verses.tsw_comparator: knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance.

verses.rationale: Keep work, completion, and wholeness connected; use mature for teleios here and explain its relation to complete/perfect in the apparatus.
verses.before: Let endurance finish its work, so that you may be complete and whole, lacking nothing.
verses.after: Let endurance carry its work through to completion, so that you become mature and whole, with nothing lacking.
verses.tsw_comparator: And let endurance have its full work, so that you may be complete and whole, lacking in nothing.

verses.rationale: Separate the request from its assurance; render reproach in familiar English without turning generosity into a promise of wealth.
verses.before: If any of you lacks wisdom, ask God, who gives generously to everyone without reproach, and it will be given to you.
verses.after: If any of you lacks wisdom, ask God for it. God gives generously to everyone without finding fault, and will give it to you.
verses.tsw_comparator: If any of you lacks wisdom, ask of God, who gives to all generously and without reproach, and it will be given to you.

verses.rationale: Choose wavering for diakrinomenos while noting doubting/divided alternatives and the link to 1:8; keep the image intact.
verses.before: But ask in faith, without being divided, because the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind.
verses.after: But ask with faith, without wavering. Anyone who wavers is like a wave at sea, blown and tossed by the wind.
verses.tsw_comparator: But ask in faith, doubting nothing; for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind.

verses.rationale: Supply the ordinary English demonstrative link to the preceding image; retain the warning without softening it.
verses.before: That person should not expect to receive anything from the Lord,
verses.after: A person like that should not expect to receive anything from the Lord.
verses.tsw_comparator: For that person should not expect to receive anything from the Lord,

verses.rationale: Render dipsychos with divided mind and the ways idiom with everything they do; preserve the same divided-language link in 4:8.
verses.before: being double-minded and unstable in all their ways.
verses.after: Their mind is divided, and they are unsteady in everything they do.
verses.tsw_comparator: being double-minded, unstable in all his ways.

verses.rationale: Make low social standing intelligible without restricting it to income; preserve boast and the upward image.
verses.before: Let the lowly brother or sister boast in being lifted up,
verses.after: Let a brother or sister of low standing boast in being raised up,
verses.tsw_comparator: Let the lowly believer boast in being lifted up,

verses.rationale: Complete the elliptical rich-person clause and separate the reason into a sentence; do not silently label the rich as believers.
verses.before: and the rich in being brought low, because the rich will pass away like a flower in the grass.
verses.after: and let the rich boast in being brought down. The rich will pass away like a flower in the grass.
verses.tsw_comparator: and the rich in being humbled, because like a flower in the grass he will pass away.

verses.rationale: Break the extended image into audible sentences; keep grass, flower, beauty, and the abrupt end during ongoing pursuits.
verses.before: The sun rises with its scorching heat and withers the grass; its flower falls and its beauty perishes. In the same way the rich will fade away in the midst of their pursuits.
verses.after: The sun rises with scorching heat and dries up the grass. Its flower falls, and its beauty is lost. That is how the rich will wither while going about their business.
verses.tsw_comparator: For the sun rises with its scorching heat and withers the grass; its flower falls, and its beauty perishes. So will the rich one fade away in the midst of his pursuits.

verses.rationale: Retain crown and trial/testing language; God makes the implied referent explicit without claiming the pinned Greek contains an explicit Lord at this point.
verses.before: Blessed is the one who endures testing, because after standing the test, that person will receive the crown of life that the Lord has promised to those who love him.
verses.after: The person who endures a trial is blessed. After passing the test, they will receive the crown of life promised to those who love God.
verses.tsw_comparator: Blessed is the one who endures testing, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life that the Lord has promised to those who love him.

verses.rationale: Use active English and clarify the subject; preserve the distinction between endurance under testing and enticement to evil.
verses.before: No one who is being tempted should say, “I am being tempted by God,” because God is not tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one.
verses.after: When tempted, no one should say, “God is tempting me.” Evil cannot tempt God, and God tempts no one.
verses.tsw_comparator: Let no one say when tempted, “I am being tempted by God,” for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one.

verses.rationale: Keep desire as the agent and the lure imagery; avoid adding an external tempter to this sentence.
verses.before: Rather, each person is tempted when drawn away and enticed by their own desire.
verses.after: Each person is tempted by their own desire, which lures them away and draws them in.
verses.tsw_comparator: But each is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire.

verses.rationale: Use two sentences while preserving the entire conception/birth/growth sequence and its later echo in 1:18.
verses.before: Then desire, after it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when fully grown, gives birth to death.
verses.after: Desire then conceives and gives birth to sin. When sin is fully grown, it gives birth to death.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then desire, having conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is fully grown, brings forth death.

verses.rationale: Use a natural English familial address and preserve the warning; dear carries agapetoi without adding another relationship.
verses.before: Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers and sisters.
verses.after: My dear brothers and sisters, do not be misled.
verses.tsw_comparator: Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers and sisters.

verses.rationale: Make the lights referent intelligible; retain the parallel gifts and the light/shadow imagery rather than replacing it with an abstract explanation.
verses.before: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shifting shadow.
verses.after: Every good gift and every perfect gift comes from above, from the Father of the heavenly lights. With him there is no change or shifting shadow.
verses.tsw_comparator: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change.

verses.rationale: Name the clear subject and use a verbal created clause; retain birth, word of truth, and the qualified firstfruits metaphor.
verses.before: By his own will he gave us birth through the word of truth, so that we might be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.
verses.after: God chose to give us birth through the word of truth, so that we would be a kind of firstfruits of all that God created.
verses.tsw_comparator: Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.

verses.rationale: Retain the three-part cadence in ordinary English; do not turn the command into an added lesson.
verses.before: Know this, my beloved brothers and sisters: everyone should be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger,
verses.after: Understand this, my dear brothers and sisters: everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to become angry.
verses.tsw_comparator: Know this, my beloved brothers and sisters: let everyone be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger,

verses.rationale: Replace the abstract produce construction with bring about while retaining the consequential genitive for a note.
verses.before: because human anger does not produce the righteousness of God.
verses.after: Human anger does not bring about the righteousness of God.
verses.tsw_comparator: for human anger does not produce the righteousness of God.

verses.rationale: Divide the imperatives for comprehension; render abundant evil with runs rampant, retain the planting image and the broad life/person sense of souls.
verses.before: Therefore, put away all filthiness and the abundance of wickedness, and receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save you.
verses.after: So put away all filth and the evil that runs rampant. Humbly welcome the word planted within you, which has the power to save you.
verses.tsw_comparator: Therefore put away all filthiness and rampant wickedness, and receive with meekness the implanted word, which has the power to save your souls.

verses.rationale: Express the doer/hearer contrast as direct verbs; preserve both action and self-deception.
verses.before: Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.
verses.after: Do what the word says. If you only listen to it, you are deceiving yourselves.
verses.tsw_comparator: But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.

verses.rationale: Keep the concrete face/mirror image and the action contrast; avoid adding an explanation about spiritual identity.
verses.before: For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, that person is like someone looking at their natural face in a mirror;
verses.after: Anyone who listens to the word but does not do what it says is like someone studying their own face in a mirror.
verses.tsw_comparator: For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks at his natural face in a mirror;

verses.rationale: Use familiar contemporary phrasing for the three actions while preserving their sequence.
verses.before: they look at themselves, go away, and immediately forget what they were like.
verses.after: They look at themselves, walk away, and at once forget what they look like.
verses.tsw_comparator: for he looks at himself and goes away, and at once forgets what kind of person he was.

verses.rationale: Place the blessing in a readable main clause, then unfold the participial contrast; retain perfect law and law of freedom.
verses.before: But the one who looks intently into the perfect law, the law of freedom, and continues in it—not becoming a hearer who forgets, but a doer who acts—will be blessed in what they do.
verses.after: But someone who looks closely into the perfect law, the law of freedom, and stays with it will be blessed in what they do. They do not listen and forget; they put it into practice.
verses.tsw_comparator: But the one who looks into the perfect law, the law of liberty, and continues in it—being not a hearer who forgets, but a doer who acts—he will be blessed in his doing.

verses.rationale: Separate the verdict; preserve the bridle/tongue image that prepares chapter 3 rather than flattening it into good manners.
verses.before: If anyone thinks they are religious but does not bridle their tongue and instead deceives their own heart, that person's religion is empty.
verses.after: Anyone who thinks they are religious but does not keep a bridle on their tongue is deceiving their own heart. Their religion is empty.
verses.tsw_comparator: If anyone thinks himself religious and does not bridle his tongue but deceives his own heart, this person’s religion is empty.

verses.rationale: Make the definition a direct English sentence; preserve the named vulnerable groups and the moral image without modern substitutions.
verses.before: Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress and to keep oneself unstained from the world.
verses.after: In the eyes of God our Father, pure and untainted religion means caring for orphans and widows in their trouble and keeping oneself unstained by the world.
verses.tsw_comparator: Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world.

verses.rationale: Use favoritism for status-based partiality and natural verbal faith language; retain the existing glory attachment and flag its compact Greek construction in a note.
verses.before: My brothers and sisters, as you hold faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ, do not show partiality.
verses.after: My brothers and sisters, do not show favoritism as you put your faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ.
verses.tsw_comparator: My brothers, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with partiality.

verses.rationale: Break the hypothetical scene into two sentences without making it a narrated historical event; retain both men and their contrasting clothing.
verses.before: Suppose a man wearing a gold ring and fine clothing comes into your gathering, and a poor man in dirty clothing also comes in.
verses.after: Imagine a man coming into your gathering with a gold ring and splendid clothes. A poor man in filthy clothes comes in too.
verses.tsw_comparator: For if a man wearing a gold ring and fine clothing comes into your assembly, and a poor man in shabby clothing also comes in,

verses.rationale: Follow the pinned SBLGNT location/order of stand or sit there; retain the degrading footstool image and note the variant behind the former wording.
verses.before: If you pay special attention to the one wearing fine clothing and say, “You sit here in a good place,” but say to the poor man, “You stand over there,” or, “Sit here at my feet,”
verses.after: You give your attention to the one in splendid clothes and say, “Here, take this good seat.” But you tell the poor man, “Stand, or sit there below my footstool.”
verses.tsw_comparator: and you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing and say, “You sit here in a good place,” while you say to the poor man, “You stand over there,” or, “Sit down at my feet,”

verses.rationale: Supply a clear link back to the hypothetical scene; keep the division/judgment accusation and evil reasoning.
verses.before: have you not made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?
verses.after: When you do that, have you not divided yourselves and become judges whose judgments are evil?
verses.tsw_comparator: have you not then made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?

verses.rationale: Turn heirs into inherit while preserving kingdom, promise, and the poor/rich reversal; name the clear divine referent.
verses.before: Listen, my beloved brothers and sisters. Has God not chosen those who are poor in the world's eyes to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom he promised to those who love him?
verses.after: Listen, my dear brothers and sisters. Did God not choose those the world regards as poor to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom promised to those who love God?
verses.tsw_comparator: Listen, my beloved brothers, has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, which he has promised to those who love him?

verses.rationale: Render oppression as the exercise of power against others; preserve direct accusation and the court action.
verses.before: But you have dishonored the poor. Is it not the rich who oppress you and drag you into court?
verses.after: Yet you have humiliated the poor. Is it not the rich who use their power against you and drag you into court?
verses.tsw_comparator: But you have dishonored the poor. Are not the rich the ones who oppress you, and the ones who drag you into court?

verses.rationale: Render blasphemy against the name in ordinary English while preserving the naming-over image; do not insert baptism into the main text.
verses.before: Are they not the ones who blaspheme the honorable name by which you were called?
verses.after: Are they not the ones who insult the honorable name spoken over you?
verses.tsw_comparator: Are they not the ones who blaspheme the honorable name by which you were called?

verses.rationale: Use a direct command within the citation; retain royal law rather than interpreting the royal relationship away.
verses.before: If you truly fulfill the royal law according to Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing well.
verses.after: If you carry out the royal law found in Scripture, “Love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing well.
verses.tsw_comparator: If you really fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing well.

verses.rationale: Turn committing sin and convicted transgressors into direct clauses; keep law as the agent of conviction.
verses.before: But if you show partiality, you are committing sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors.
verses.after: But if you show favoritism, you sin. The law finds you guilty of breaking it.
verses.tsw_comparator: But if you show partiality, you are committing sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors.

verses.rationale: Preserve the whole/one contrast and accountability, using obeys as ordinary English for keeping the law.
verses.before: Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at one point has become accountable for all of it.
verses.after: Whoever obeys the whole law but stumbles at just one point is accountable for breaking it all.
verses.tsw_comparator: For whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it.

verses.rationale: Keep the shared speaker and both prohibitions; make the conditional conclusion easier to follow.
verses.before: For the one who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” If you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law.
verses.after: The one who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” Even if you do not commit adultery, you have broken the law if you murder.
verses.tsw_comparator: For he who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” If you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law.

verses.rationale: Connect speech and action in a single direct sentence; preserve judgment and the recurring law of freedom phrase.
verses.before: So speak and act as people who are going to be judged by the law of freedom.
verses.after: Let your words and actions be those of people who will be judged by the law of freedom.
verses.tsw_comparator: So speak and so act as those who are to be judged under the law of freedom.

verses.rationale: Recast the first clause around its human subject; retain the forceful final sentence unchanged because it is clear and carries the argument.
verses.before: For judgment will be without mercy to the one who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.
verses.after: Anyone who has shown no mercy will face judgment without mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.
verses.tsw_comparator: For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.

verses.rationale: Use deeds consistently for erga throughout the argument; preserve the question about the faith just claimed, not an abstract denial of faith.
verses.before: What good is it, my brothers and sisters, if someone says they have faith but do not have works? Can that kind of faith save them?
verses.after: My brothers and sisters, what good is it if someone claims to have faith but has no deeds? Can that kind of faith save them?
verses.tsw_comparator: What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?

verses.rationale: Make the conditional example readable as a complete sentence; keep the embodied material need.
verses.before: If a brother or sister has nothing to wear and lacks daily food,
verses.after: Suppose a brother or sister has no clothes and not enough food for the day.
verses.tsw_comparator: If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking daily food,

verses.rationale: Separate the empty blessing from the question; retain the body's needs rather than turning the scene into a general moral principle.
verses.before: and one of you says, “Go in peace; keep warm and eat well,” but you do not give them what the body needs, what good is that?
verses.after: One of you says, “Go in peace! Stay warm and eat your fill.” If you do not give them what their body needs, what good have you done?
verses.tsw_comparator: and one of you says to them, “Go in peace, be warmed and filled,” without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that?

verses.rationale: Use the same deeds term and keep the stark verdict, without inserting merely apparent or false before faith.
verses.before: In the same way, faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.
verses.after: So faith on its own, without deeds, is dead.
verses.tsw_comparator: So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.

verses.rationale: Keep the inherited quotation boundary while flagging disputed speaker boundaries; use a verb for the final erga without losing the repeated faith/deeds contrast.
verses.before: But someone will say, “You have faith, and I have works.” Show me your faith apart from works, and I will show you my faith by my works.
verses.after: But someone will say, “You have faith; I have deeds.” Show me your faith without deeds, and I will show you my faith through what I do.
verses.tsw_comparator: But someone will say, “You have faith and I have works.” Show me your faith apart from your works, and I will show you my faith by my works.

verses.rationale: Use an audible rhetorical question and short response; preserve the monotheistic confession and the demonic counterexample.
verses.before: You believe that God is one. You do well. Even the demons believe—and shudder.
verses.after: You believe that God is one? Good! Even the demons believe that, and they tremble.
verses.tsw_comparator: You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and shudder!

verses.rationale: Retain the challenge and SBLGNT useless rather than the dead variant; preserve the distinction from 2:17 and 2:26.
verses.before: Do you want to know, you foolish person, that faith apart from works is useless?
verses.after: You foolish person, do you want to see that faith without deeds is useless?
verses.tsw_comparator: Do you want to be shown, you foolish person, that faith apart from works is useless?

verses.rationale: Retain the consequential set right choice with explicit alternatives in the note; keep father, son, altar, and the by-deeds claim intact.
verses.before: Was not Abraham our father set right by works when he offered his son Isaac on the altar?
verses.after: Was our father Abraham not set right by his deeds when he offered his son Isaac on the altar?
verses.tsw_comparator: Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar?

verses.rationale: Make the cooperation and completion claims two sentences; link maturity to teleios in 1:4 without subordinating deeds to a Pauline explanation.
verses.before: You see that faith was working together with his works, and through the works faith was brought to completion.
verses.after: You can see that his faith worked together with his deeds. Through those deeds, his faith reached maturity.
verses.tsw_comparator: You see that faith was working together with his works, and by works faith was brought to completion,

verses.rationale: Retain the citation's righteousness and crediting language; use believed in continuity with the faith vocabulary and split the friendship clause.
verses.before: And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham trusted God, and it was counted to him as righteousness,” and he was called a friend of God.
verses.after: This fulfilled the Scripture that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.” He was also called God's friend.
verses.tsw_comparator: and the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”—and he was called a friend of God.

verses.rationale: Retain the explicit conclusion and existing dikaioo choice; do not replace it with only shown to already be righteous.
verses.before: You see that a person is set right by works and not by faith alone.
verses.after: You see, then, that a person is set right by deeds, and not by faith alone.
verses.tsw_comparator: You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.

verses.rationale: Unfold the parallel example without hiding Rahab's description or adding a motive; retain the same set right/deeds wording.
verses.before: In the same way, was not Rahab the prostitute also set right by works when she welcomed the messengers and sent them out by another way?
verses.after: Was it not the same with Rahab the prostitute? She too was set right by deeds when she welcomed the messengers and sent them away by a different route.
verses.tsw_comparator: And in the same way was not also Rahab the prostitute justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way?

verses.rationale: Use parallel English clauses and retain spirit, with the breath alternative in the apparatus.
verses.before: For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead.
verses.after: Just as a body is dead without the spirit, faith is dead without deeds.
verses.tsw_comparator: For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead.

verses.rationale: Split warning and reason; preserve James's inclusion of himself among teachers.
verses.before: Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers and sisters, because you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly.
verses.after: My brothers and sisters, not many of you should become teachers. You know that those of us who teach will face a stricter judgment.
verses.tsw_comparator: Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness.

verses.rationale: Keep stumble and bridle metaphors; link mature with 1:4 and 2:22 instead of treating it as a new unrelated quality.
verses.before: We all stumble in many ways. If anyone does not stumble in what they say, that person is complete, able to bridle the whole body as well.
verses.after: All of us stumble in many ways. Anyone who never stumbles in speech is fully mature and can bridle their whole body too.
verses.tsw_comparator: For we all stumble in many ways. And if anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect man, able also to bridle his whole body.

verses.rationale: Use a concrete action sentence with the purpose and result visible; retain the bodily control image.
verses.before: When we put bits into horses' mouths so that they obey us, we guide their whole bodies.
verses.after: We put bits in horses' mouths to make them obey us, and so we can turn their whole bodies.
verses.tsw_comparator: If we put bits into the mouths of horses so that they obey us, we guide their whole bodies as well.

verses.rationale: Split the invitation to notice from the image; use ordinary sailing language without introducing modern machinery.
verses.before: Or consider ships: though they are so large and driven by strong winds, they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the pilot wants to go.
verses.after: Think of ships too. They are large and driven by fierce winds, yet a tiny rudder turns them wherever the person steering wants to go.
verses.tsw_comparator: Or look at ships: eventhough they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs.

verses.rationale: Preserve the two linked small/large comparisons and boast language; make the exclamation audible.
verses.before: In the same way, the tongue is a small part of the body, yet it boasts of great things. See how small a fire can set such a great forest ablaze.
verses.after: The tongue is like that: a small part of the body that makes great boasts. Look how a little fire sets a whole forest ablaze!
verses.tsw_comparator: So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire!

verses.rationale: Break the dense syntax into sentences without losing any of the images; retain Gehenna and document the difficult course-of-life expression.
verses.before: The tongue is also a fire, a world of unrighteousness among our members. It stains the whole body, sets the course of life on fire, and is itself set on fire by Gehenna.
verses.after: The tongue is a fire too. Among the parts of our body, it is a world of wrongdoing. It stains the whole body and sets the entire course of life ablaze, while Gehenna itself sets it on fire.
verses.tsw_comparator: And the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness. The tongue is set among our members, staining the whole body, setting on fire the course of life, and set on fire by hell.

verses.rationale: Make humans the subject of the passive Greek construction; preserve both present activity and accomplished taming.
verses.before: Every kind of animal and bird, reptile and sea creature, can be tamed and has been tamed by humankind,
verses.after: Human beings tame, and have tamed, every kind of wild animal, bird, reptile, and sea creature.
verses.tsw_comparator: For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, can be tamed and has been tamed by mankind,

verses.rationale: Keep the contrast and poison image; render restless/unstable with unruly in this context.
verses.before: but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
verses.after: Yet no human being can tame the tongue. It is an unruly evil, filled with deadly poison.
verses.tsw_comparator: but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.

verses.rationale: Name the tongue to connect the pronoun with its image; preserve bless, curse, and divine likeness together.
verses.before: With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God.
verses.after: We use our tongues to bless the Lord and Father, and to curse people made in God's likeness.
verses.tsw_comparator: With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God.

verses.rationale: Keep the same-mouth contradiction and direct familial rebuke in natural word order.
verses.before: Blessing and cursing come from the same mouth. My brothers and sisters, this should not be.
verses.after: Out of one mouth come both blessing and cursing. My brothers and sisters, it should not be this way.
verses.tsw_comparator: From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.

verses.rationale: Use a simple question while retaining both kinds of water and the single source.
verses.before: Does a spring pour out both fresh and bitter water from the same opening?
verses.after: Can fresh water and bitter water flow from the same opening in a spring?
verses.tsw_comparator: Does a spring pour forth from the same opening both fresh and bitter water?

verses.rationale: Preserve the paired impossible fruits and the return to water; do not replace the images with their lesson.
verses.before: Can a fig tree, my brothers and sisters, produce olives, or a grapevine produce figs? Neither can salt water produce fresh water.
verses.after: My brothers and sisters, can a fig tree bear olives, or a vine bear figs? Neither can salt water yield fresh water.
verses.tsw_comparator: Can a fig tree, my brothers, bear olives, or a grapevine produce figs? Neither can a salt spring yield fresh water.

verses.rationale: Use direct address for the third-person exhortation; preserve deeds, conduct, and the wisdom/gentleness relationship.
verses.before: Who among you is wise and understanding? Let that person show by good conduct their works done in the gentleness of wisdom.
verses.after: Who among you is wise and understanding? Show it through a good life and deeds done with the gentleness that wisdom brings.
verses.tsw_comparator: Who is wise and understanding among you? By his good conduct let him show his works in the meekness of wisdom.

verses.rationale: Use a concrete English predicate for the inner conditions; retain the prohibition and truth contrast.
verses.before: But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and lie against the truth.
verses.after: But if your hearts hold bitter jealousy and selfish ambition, do not boast and deny the truth.
verses.tsw_comparator: But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and be false to the truth.

verses.rationale: Provide an explicit backward reference while preserving all three severe descriptions.
verses.before: This is not the wisdom that comes down from above. It is earthly, unspiritual, demonic.
verses.after: Wisdom like that does not come from above. It is earthly, unspiritual, and demonic.
verses.tsw_comparator: This is not the wisdom that comes down from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic.

verses.rationale: Make the relationship readable without adding a new moral category or an external cause.
verses.before: For wherever jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there is disorder and every kind of evil practice.
verses.after: Where jealousy and selfish ambition take hold, disorder and every kind of evil follow.
verses.tsw_comparator: For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice.

verses.rationale: Make eupeithes intelligible as open to persuasion; retain good fruit and the disputed impartial choice with its alternatives noted.
verses.before: But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, willing to yield, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere.
verses.after: Wisdom from above is pure first of all. It is also peace-loving, considerate, open to persuasion, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial, and free of hypocrisy.
verses.tsw_comparator: But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere.

verses.rationale: Use active English while retaining the unusual sowing-a-harvest image; note the alternative dative reading for peacemakers instead of by peacemakers.
verses.before: And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.
verses.after: Those who make peace sow a harvest of righteousness in peace.
verses.tsw_comparator: And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

verses.rationale: Distinguish hedonai/pleasures from the desire term of chapter 1; keep both communal conflict and the bodily warfare metaphor.
verses.before: Where do the conflicts and fights among you come from? Do they not come from your desires that are at war within you?
verses.after: What causes the wars and quarrels among you? Is it not the pleasures you crave, waging war within your bodies?
verses.tsw_comparator: What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you?

verses.rationale: Follow the sequence of the pinned Greek without adding so between wanting and murder; note the punctuation question and retain murder without softening it.
verses.before: You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and wage war. You do not have because you do not ask.
verses.after: You want what you do not have. You murder and covet, but cannot get what you want. You quarrel and wage war. You do not have because you do not ask.
verses.tsw_comparator: You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel. You do not have because you do not ask.

verses.rationale: Make the spending object explicit from context; retain wrong asking and pleasure rather than implying all requests are condemned.
verses.before: You ask and do not receive because you ask with wrong motives, so that you can spend it on your desires.
verses.after: You ask but do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives: you want to spend what you receive on your pleasures.
verses.tsw_comparator: You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions.

verses.rationale: Retain the marital accusation and friendship/enmity contrast; do not substitute a modern political identity for world.
verses.before: You adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Whoever chooses to be a friend of the world makes themselves an enemy of God.
verses.after: You adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world means hostility toward God? Anyone who wants to be the world's friend becomes God's enemy.
verses.tsw_comparator: You adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.

verses.rationale: Retain the existing God-subject reading in clearer English; keep the major spirit-subject alternative and uncertain citation identification in the note.
verses.before: Or do you think Scripture speaks for no reason when it says, “He yearns jealously for the spirit he has caused to dwell in us”?
verses.after: Or do you think Scripture speaks empty words when it says, “God longs jealously for the spirit he made to live in us”?
verses.tsw_comparator: Or do you suppose it is to no purpose that the Scripture says, “He yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us”?

verses.rationale: Clarify the subject and connective; keep the memorable scriptural quotation rather than varying it for distinctness.
verses.before: But he gives greater grace. Therefore Scripture says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”
verses.after: But God gives greater grace. That is why Scripture says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”
verses.tsw_comparator: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”

verses.rationale: Use familiar verbs for resisting and fleeing while preserving the imperative and promised result.
verses.before: Therefore submit yourselves to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
verses.after: So submit yourselves to God. Stand against the devil, and he will run from you.
verses.tsw_comparator: Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.

verses.rationale: Retain the reciprocal approach, hands/hearts imagery, and the divided-mind link to 1:8.
verses.before: Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.
verses.after: Come close to God, and God will come close to you. Wash your hands, you sinners; purify your hearts, you whose minds are divided.
verses.tsw_comparator: Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.

verses.rationale: Retain the dense lament imperatives without expanding them into an instruction to sustain misery indefinitely.
verses.before: Be miserable, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom.
verses.after: Grieve, mourn, and weep. Turn your laughter into mourning and your joy into sorrow.
verses.tsw_comparator: Be wretched and mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom.

verses.rationale: Use ordinary English for before/exalt; preserve the down/up movement and explicit divine agency.
verses.before: Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.
verses.after: Humble yourselves in the Lord's presence, and the Lord will lift you up.
verses.tsw_comparator: Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.

verses.rationale: Unfold the repeated law/judgment argument into three sentences; connect doing the law with hearing/doing in chapter 1.
verses.before: Do not speak against one another, brothers and sisters. The one who speaks against a brother or sister or judges them speaks against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but its judge.
verses.after: Brothers and sisters, do not speak against one another. If you speak against or judge a brother or sister, you speak against the law and judge it. When you judge the law, you sit as its judge instead of doing what it says.
verses.tsw_comparator: Do not speak evil against one another, brothers. The one who speaks against a brother or judges his brother, speaks evil against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge.

verses.rationale: Preserve the singular authority and the sharp final question without naming a human lawgiver.
verses.before: There is one lawgiver and judge, the one who is able to save and destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?
verses.after: There is only one lawgiver and judge, who can save and destroy. Who are you to judge your neighbor?
verses.tsw_comparator: There is one lawgiver and judge, he who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?

verses.rationale: Use a natural address to the imagined merchants; preserve time, city, duration, trade, and profit.
verses.before: Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go to such-and-such a city, spend a year there, conduct business, and make a profit.”
verses.after: Now listen, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go to a certain city, spend a year there trading, and make a profit.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit”—

verses.rationale: Follow the compact Greek tomorrow/life construction in a clear sentence; preserve the mist image rather than replacing it with a mortality explanation.
verses.before: Yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? You are a mist that appears for a little while and then disappears.
verses.after: You do not even know what your life will be like tomorrow. You are a mist, visible for a moment and then gone.
verses.tsw_comparator: yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes.

verses.rationale: Keep both living and acting under the condition; do not reduce the sentence to a pious formula about plans only.
verses.before: Instead you should say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.”
verses.after: Instead, say, “If the Lord wishes, we will live and do this or that.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Instead you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.”

verses.rationale: Render alazoneiai as arrogant claims and retain the condemnation of this particular boasting.
verses.before: As it is, you boast in your arrogance. All such boasting is evil.
verses.after: But you take pride in your arrogant claims. All boasting of that kind is evil.
verses.tsw_comparator: As it is, you boast in your arrogance. All such boasting is evil.

verses.rationale: Express omitted action directly while preserving knowledge, good action, omission, and sin.
verses.before: So whoever knows the right thing to do and does not do it, for that person it is sin.
verses.after: So if you know the good you should do and leave it undone, you sin.
verses.tsw_comparator: So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin.

verses.rationale: Preserve the prophetic direct address and approaching misery; use an audible English summons.
verses.before: Come now, you rich people: weep and wail over the miseries that are coming upon you.
verses.after: Now listen, you rich people. Weep and cry out over the suffering that is coming upon you.
verses.tsw_comparator: Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you.

verses.rationale: Split the paired decay images and use an active moth clause without adding a time or cause.
verses.before: Your riches have rotted, and your clothes have become moth-eaten.
verses.after: Your wealth has rotted away. Moths have eaten your clothes.
verses.tsw_comparator: Your riches have rotted and your garments are moth-eaten.

verses.rationale: Retain the existing fire attachment while noting the pinned edition's alternative punctuation; preserve flesh, corrosion, hoarding, and last days.
verses.before: Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will testify against you and eat your flesh like fire. You have stored up treasure in the last days.
verses.after: Your gold and silver are corroded. Their corrosion will stand as evidence against you and eat your flesh like fire. You have piled up treasure in the last days.
verses.tsw_comparator: Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be evidence against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have stored up treasure in the last days.

verses.rationale: Put the withholding accusation in a direct sentence; retain the personified wages, divine ears, and title explained in a note.
verses.before: Look! The wages you withheld from the workers who harvested your fields are crying out, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts.
verses.after: Look! You have held back the wages of those who harvested your fields, and those wages cry out. The harvesters' cries have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts.
verses.tsw_comparator: Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, cry out, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts.

verses.rationale: Retain hearts and slaughter rather than replacing them with an explanation; use on for en instead of silently importing a future-oriented for.
verses.before: You have lived on the earth in luxury and self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts for a day of slaughter.
verses.after: You have spent your lives on earth in luxury and indulgence. You have fattened your hearts on a day of slaughter.
verses.tsw_comparator: You have lived on the earth in luxury and in self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter.

verses.rationale: Preserve the singular figure and inherited declarative reading; note that the pinned edition punctuates the final clause as a question.
verses.before: You have condemned and murdered the righteous person, who does not resist you.
verses.after: You have condemned the righteous person and put that person to death. The righteous person does not resist you.
verses.tsw_comparator: You have condemned and murdered the righteous person. He does not resist you.

verses.rationale: Unfold the agricultural waiting in ordinary English; retain patience, crop, both seasonal rains, and the Lord's coming.
verses.before: Therefore be patient, brothers and sisters, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient for it until it receives the early and late rains.
verses.after: So be patient, brothers and sisters, until the Lord comes. Think of a farmer waiting patiently for the land's precious crop and for the early and late rains.
verses.tsw_comparator: Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it, until it receives the early and the late rains.

verses.rationale: Preserve bodily heart imagery and the strengthening command; retain the text's temporal urgency without adding a timetable.
verses.before: You also must be patient. Strengthen your hearts, because the coming of the Lord is near.
verses.after: You too must be patient and make your hearts firm, because the Lord's coming is near.
verses.tsw_comparator: You also, be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is near.

verses.rationale: Use ordinary complaint language while preserving the judgment warning and vivid door image.
verses.before: Do not grumble against one another, brothers and sisters, so that you may not be judged. Look—the Judge is standing at the door.
verses.after: Brothers and sisters, do not complain against one another, or you will face judgment. Look! The judge is standing at the door.
verses.tsw_comparator: Do not grumble against one another, brothers, so that you may not be judged; behold, the Judge is standing at the door.

verses.rationale: Reorder the example so its subject and purpose can be followed on one hearing; preserve the prophets' authority and suffering.
verses.before: As an example of suffering and patience, brothers and sisters, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.
verses.after: Brothers and sisters, take the prophets who spoke in the Lord's name as your example of patience in suffering.
verses.tsw_comparator: As an example of suffering and patience, brothers, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.

verses.rationale: Render telos as outcome while noting purpose/end alternatives; keep endurance, Job, blessing, and the compassionate Lord.
verses.before: Look, we call those blessed who endured. You have heard of Job's endurance and have seen the Lord's purpose in the end—that the Lord is deeply compassionate and merciful.
verses.after: We call those who endured blessed. You have heard how Job endured, and you have seen the outcome the Lord brought about. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy.
verses.tsw_comparator: Behold, we consider those blessed who remained steadfast. You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the outcome of the Lord, that the Lord is compassionate and merciful.

verses.rationale: Make swearing clearly refer to oaths rather than profanity; preserve the yes/no instruction and judicial consequence.
verses.before: Above all, my brothers and sisters, do not swear—not by heaven, earth, or any other oath. Let your “yes” be yes and your “no” be no, so that you do not fall under judgment.
verses.after: Above all, my brothers and sisters, do not take oaths by heaven or earth, or swear any other oath. Let your yes mean yes and your no mean no, so that you do not come under judgment.
verses.tsw_comparator: But above all, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath, but let your “yes” be yes and your “no” be no, so that you may not fall under judgment.

verses.rationale: Use concise direct imperatives for the Greek third-person commands while retaining both community circumstances.
verses.before: Is anyone among you suffering? Let that person pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let that person sing praise.
verses.after: Is anyone among you suffering? Pray. Is anyone in good spirits? Sing praise.
verses.tsw_comparator: Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise.

verses.rationale: Resolve the confusing chain of them pronouns; preserve elders, prayer, oil, and divine name without deciding the anointing's mechanism.
verses.before: Is anyone among you sick? Let that person call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over them, anointing them with oil in the name of the Lord.
verses.after: Is anyone among you sick? Call the church's elders. They should pray over the sick person and anoint that person with oil in the Lord's name.
verses.tsw_comparator: Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord.

verses.rationale: Keep save and raise distinct and retain the conditional presence of sins; avoid turning illness into proof of sin or promising a medical mechanism.
verses.before: The prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise them up. And if they have committed sins, they will be forgiven.
verses.after: Prayer offered in faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise that person up. Any sins they have committed will be forgiven.
verses.tsw_comparator: And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.

verses.rationale: Preserve mutual confession/prayer and the healing purpose; leave the participle's agency open and record the energized/effective alternatives.
verses.before: Therefore confess your sins to one another and pray for one another so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person is very powerful in its effect.
verses.after: So confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be healed. A righteous person's prayer has great power as it works.
verses.tsw_comparator: Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working.

verses.rationale: Make like nature intelligible and retain the intensive prayer idiom, land, and exact duration.
verses.before: Elijah was a human being with a nature like ours, and he prayed earnestly that it would not rain. It did not rain on the land for three years and six months.
verses.after: Elijah was human, just like us. He prayed earnestly for no rain, and no rain fell on the land for three years and six months.
verses.tsw_comparator: Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain, and for three years and six months it did not rain on the earth.

verses.rationale: Retain the heaven/earth agricultural pairing in natural English without supplying an unstated cause beyond the sequence.
verses.before: Then he prayed again, and heaven gave rain, and the earth produced its fruit.
verses.after: He prayed again. The sky gave rain, and the land brought forth its crop.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then he prayed again, and heaven gave rain, and the earth bore its fruit.

verses.rationale: Retain the unfinished conditional leading into 5:20 and the communal scope; do not end the thought at a verse boundary.
verses.before: My brothers and sisters, if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone brings that person back,
verses.after: My brothers and sisters, if one of you wanders from the truth and someone brings that person back,
verses.tsw_comparator: My brothers, if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone brings him back,

verses.rationale: Preserve turning, way, life/death, and covering; retain the open life referent and note the Greek possessive rather than silently erasing its ambiguity.
verses.before: know that whoever brings a sinner back from the error of their way will save a life from death and cover a multitude of sins.
verses.after: remember this: whoever turns a sinner back from a wandering path will save a life from death and cover many sins.
verses.tsw_comparator: let him know that whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.
